title: kirtan repertoire (20 songs)
hook: a line sung back slower than it went out, and the old hymn that bows to the potter and the carpenter

segments.voice: Yesterday, kirtan repertoire: the first song of the night, to Ganesha, clearing the road. Did you name an obstacle before you began something? Day nine hundred eighty-eight.

The leader sings it quickly the first time, almost spoken. Om namah shivaya. The room sends it back a little slower. The leader slows to meet them. After a while nobody is rushing, and the line has stretched out like a rope being let down a well. There's no verse to remember, no chorus, no bridge. Just those few syllables, over and over, while the drum keeps time underneath. It's a simple song to learn. Its words, though, reach back into one of the old Vedic hymns.
screen: `SUNG FAST, SENT BACK SLOW.` → `NO VERSE, NO CHORUS.` → `A LINE FROM AN OLD HYMN.`

segments.voice: Om namah shivaya. Namah is a bow, a salutation: I bow, honor to. Shivaya is to Shiva, a name that also carries the sense of the kind one, the auspicious one. Put together: Om, I bow to Shiva. The words namah shivaya appear in the Shri Rudram, a long hymn to Rudra, the fierce form of Shiva, in the Krishna Yajur Veda. There they come in a line that bows to him twice over: to the kind one, and to the one who is kinder still, both names for the same Rudra. But the setting around that line is the surprise. The Rudram bows over and over, and it bows to Shiva in places you wouldn't expect. In the hunter, in the potter, in the carpenter, the chariot maker. In the forest, in the field, in the flowing water. In some lines it even names the lord of thieves. The hymn seems determined not to leave anything out. So the little kirtan line arrives carrying a whole world with it. When a group sings om namah shivaya, they're singing a phrase that once sat in a hymn bowing to every corner of life. That's worth knowing when the line comes round yet again. Repetition here isn't the same thing said again. Each time the room sends it back, it can be a bow to something different: the person beside you, the tired body, the noise from the street, the thing you don't want to face. Shaivas, the Hindus who worship Shiva as the highest, hold this mantra very close. But people from other Hindu homes sing it at kirtan too, and a newcomer can join in by the second round.
screen: `NAMAH: I BOW. SHIVAYA: TO SHIVA.` · `THE WORDS COME FROM THE RUDRAM.` · `THE HYMN BOWS TO EVERYONE.` · `EACH ROUND, A DIFFERENT BOW.` · then, large: `OM NAMAH SHIVAYA.`

segments.voice: Let the hands rest and the jaw loosen. On the out-breath, say the line silently, or aloud if you're alone: om namah shivaya. Each time it comes round, let it be a bow to one thing nearby. The chair holding you. The sound in the next room. Your own hands. Someone you'll see later today. If you pray, let the line be your prayer. If not, let it simply be a way of noticing, one thing at a time. The bell holds the time.
Kirtan repertoire. Today's song: om namah shivaya, I bow to Shiva, a line that comes from a hymn that bows to everything.
Your line: kirtan repertoire, twenty songs. Today, choose one ordinary worker you pass, a driver, a cook, a cleaner, and give them a small silent bow. Day nine hundred eighty-eight.

howItsDone: At a kirtan, om namah shivaya is sung as a simple call-and-response line, often slowing over many rounds; Shaiva Hindus also repeat it as a mantra in daily japa.
